passage:
I sit behind Chaitanya in Class 5, so I saw it all. On Lalit's first day, Chaitanya said hi and Lalit just looked at his shoes and said nothing. At lunch Chaitanya told us, "The new boy is rude. Don't talk to him."
Since then Lalit has shared his colour pencils with half the class, helped Rinku find her lost bottle, and laughed at all of Chaitanya's jokes. Last week he even saved Chaitanya a seat at assembly. Chaitanya sat somewhere else. "He's only pretending," Chaitanya said. "I saw what he's really like on day one."
I don't know what goes on in Chaitanya's head. But I think Lalit was just scared that first day. I was scared on my first day too.

qa.q: What did Lalit do for Chaitanya last week?
qa.a: He saved Chaitanya a seat at assembly.

qa.q: Why does Chaitanya think Lalit is only pretending?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt snubbed and hurt on day one and decided Lalit was rude, so every kind thing since then gets explained away to fit that first story.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya try in order to see Lalit more fairly?
qa.a: Count what Lalit has done since the first day, and maybe ask Lalit how that first day felt.

qa.q: How does the narrator see Lalit's first day?
qa.a: The narrator thinks Lalit was just scared, remembering being scared on a first day too.

grounding: It shows a child holding on to a first-day opinion of a new classmate even though his later behaviour is kind.

passage:
Monday. The new girl, Aparna, answered every question in maths and English. Rukmini, ten, rolled her eyes at her friend Pinky. "Show-off," she whispered.
Thursday. In PT, Aparna fell in the relay and laughed at herself. At lunch she asked Rukmini how to do the Hindi homework, because her old school never taught Hindi. Rukmini explained quickly and turned away. "She's just acting humble," she told Pinky.
The next Tuesday. Aparna brought a box of homemade laddoos for the whole row, Rukmini included. Rukmini ate one. It was delicious. "She still thinks she's the smartest," Rukmini muttered, though she couldn't say what Aparna had done that week to make her think so.

qa.q: What did Aparna bring the next Tuesday?
qa.a: A box of homemade laddoos for the whole row.

qa.q: Why does Rukmini call Aparna's humble behaviour acting?
qa.a: Rukmini made up her mind on Monday that Aparna was a show-off, so humble or kind actions later get squeezed into that first picture.

qa.q: What question could Rukmini ask herself about Aparna?
qa.a: "What has Aparna actually done this week?" Answering honestly might loosen the Monday opinion.

qa.q: What might the first week have felt like for Aparna?
qa.a: Aparna was new, didn't know Hindi and fell in PT, so she was probably trying hard to make friends and might be hurt if she noticed Rukmini turning away.

grounding: It shows a child judging a new classmate on the first day and keeping that view despite later behaviour.

passage: Siddharth, you've decided the new boy in your class is a cheat because of one test on his first day? Let your Pradeep Chacha tell you about Gopal. When I was eleven, in our school in Meerut, a new boy came in the middle of the year. On his first day he looked at my answer sheet during the spelling test. From that moment, Gopal was "the cheat" to me. He lent me his umbrella in the rain, and I thought, trying to buy friends. He topped science on his own, and I thought, must have copied. It took me a whole year, and a school trip where he helped me when I got lost, to see that his first day was just a scared boy at a new school. We're still friends. One day told me almost nothing about him.

qa.q: What did Gopal do during the spelling test on his first day?
qa.a: He looked at Chacha's answer sheet.

qa.q: Why did young Pradeep think Gopal was trying to buy friends with the umbrella?
qa.a: Having labelled Gopal 'the cheat' on day one, young Pradeep felt suspicious and read every kind act through that first label.

qa.q: What is Chacha hoping Siddharth will do about the new boy?
qa.a: Wait before deciding, and notice what the new boy does over the coming weeks instead of judging him by one test.

qa.q: How does Chacha now see Gopal's first day?
qa.a: As a scared boy at a new school, not a cheat.

grounding: It shows a child whose first-day opinion of a new classmate held for a year despite later kindness.

passage:
The monsoon had flooded the school ground in Bhopal, so Class 5 was stuck indoors for the whole week, and the new boy, Tarun, joined on Monday.
On Monday he cried at the gate when his mother left. Nilesh, ten, whispered to the others, "Crybaby. He's going to be so annoying."
On Tuesday, with no PT, Tarun showed the class how to fold paper into a working frog. On Wednesday, when the lights went out in the storm, he was the one who calmed the little ones in the next room with a story. On Thursday he lent Nilesh his extra pencil without being asked.
On Friday, the teacher asked who wanted to be Tarun's partner for the rain-gauge project. Half the class put up their hands.
Nilesh didn't. "He cried on Monday," he said, loud enough for everyone.

qa.q: What did Tarun lend Nilesh on Thursday?
qa.a: He lent Nilesh his extra pencil without being asked.

qa.q: Why does Nilesh still think of Tarun as a crybaby by Friday?
qa.a: His first picture of Tarun was formed on Monday at the gate, and it feels like the real story, so the paper frogs, the calming story and the pencil don't change it for him.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do on Friday to give Tarun a fair chance?
qa.a: He could think back over the whole week instead of just Monday, and try being Tarun's partner to see what he is really like now.

qa.q: What is it like for Tarun to hear "He cried on Monday" in front of everyone?
qa.a: It would feel embarrassing and unfair, since Tarun has spent the whole week being kind and helpful and is still judged by his hardest first moment.

grounding: It shows a child forming an opinion of a new classmate on the first day and sticking to it though his later behaviour is different.

passage:
The new family moved into C-block of the Chennai housing colony on a Sunday. That evening Yusuf, nine, and his friends were playing football on the tar court when the new boy, Abhinav, walked across the middle of their game and kicked the ball over the wall.
"He's mean," Yusuf told everyone. "Did it on purpose."
The next week Abhinav brought the ball back, cleaned, with a note: "Sorry, I didn't know you were playing." On Wednesday he found Yusuf's lost cycle key near the gate and handed it to the watchman. On Saturday he offered to be goalkeeper, the job nobody wanted.
Yusuf still passed him the ball last, and when his sister asked why, he said, "Because he's mean. Remember the first day?"
"That was one kick," she said.
"It was the first kick," Yusuf said, as if that settled it.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do with the ball the next week?
qa.a: He brought the ball back, cleaned, with a note saying sorry.

qa.q: How does Yusuf feel about Abhinav, even after the apology and the kind acts?
qa.a: Yusuf still feels resentful toward Abhinav because of the first kick, passing him the ball last and insisting "he's mean" despite the cleaned ball, the note and the found key.

qa.q: What could Yusuf try, now that Abhinav has offered to keep goal?
qa.a: He could give Abhinav a proper turn with the ball and notice how he plays, letting what happens now count as much as the first day.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel being passed the ball last every time?
qa.a: Abhinav would likely feel left out and confused, since he apologised, returned the key and took the job nobody wanted.

grounding: It shows a child forming an opinion of a new boy on the first day and holding on to it though his later behaviour is different.

passage: Zubin, you've decided the new boy is a show-off because of one day? Let your Mahima nani tell you about Farida. When I was ten, a new girl joined our class in Jabalpur. On her very first day, she knocked my ink bottle over my copy and didn't say sorry. That was it. For me, Farida was rude. In the weeks after, she shared her tiffin with everyone, helped the little ones cross the road, even lent me a pen. I told myself she was just showing off. Months later, our teacher told us Farida had been so frightened that first day that she couldn't speak at all. My ears burned. One day, and I had written her whole story. We became friends after that, and she still sends me mangoes every summer.

qa.q: What did Farida do on her first day?
qa.a: She knocked the ink bottle over Mahima's copy and didn't say sorry.

qa.q: Why did young Mahima explain away Farida's kindness as showing off?
qa.a: Mahima felt annoyed and sure about Farida after the ink, so later kindness just seemed to prove the first story instead of changing it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nani's story?
qa.a: The teacher explaining that Farida had been too frightened to speak that first day, which showed the first impression had been wrong.

qa.q: What might that first day have been like for Farida?
qa.a: Farida was new and frightened, so scared that she couldn't speak, let alone say sorry for the ink.

grounding: Shows a child forming an opinion of a new classmate on day one and holding it despite later kindness.

passage: On the first day of Class 4, the new boy, Yusuf, grabbed the last seat by the window before Pallavi could reach it. "He's so selfish," she told her best friend at lunch. Two weeks later, the monsoon kept everyone indoors, and a flustered substitute teacher paired children for the model project due on Friday. Pallavi got Yusuf. She groaned out loud. Over the next days Yusuf brought his own glue, cut all the cardboard, and when Pallavi's volcano cracked on Thursday, he stayed through lunch fixing it. On Friday their model won a star. "He was probably still showing off," Pallavi told her mother that evening. Then she stopped. Her mother waited. "Maybe he just really likes windows," Pallavi said slowly.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do on the first day of Class 4?
qa.a: He grabbed the last seat by the window before Pallavi could reach it.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi still call Yusuf a show-off after he fixed the volcano?
qa.a: Pallavi felt so sure of her first-day opinion that his helpfulness seemed to fit it, and changing her mind felt uncomfortable.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do when a first impression feels strong?
qa.a: She could notice it came from just one day and keep track of what the person does later, like the glue, the cardboard and the fixed volcano.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have felt working with someone who groaned at being paired with him?
qa.a: Yusuf may have felt unwelcome, yet kept helping, which shows a side of him Pallavi missed at first.

grounding: Shows a child holding a first-day opinion of a new classmate even while the classmate behaves very differently later.

passage: The day Anirban's family moved into the fourth floor of their Salt Lake building, he cried at the colony gate while his mother argued with the movers. Rehana, eleven, watched from the swing. "Crybaby," she told the others. Weeks passed. Anirban turned out to be the fastest runner in the colony. He carried old Mr Sen's bags up four flights without being asked. When a stray dog cornered the little ones, he was the one who stood in front and shooed it away. Still, whenever teams were picked, Rehana said, "Not the crybaby." One evening her cousin asked, "Which crybaby?" Rehana pointed. Her cousin laughed. "That kid? He's the bravest one here." Rehana opened her mouth to argue and found she had nothing but that first day.

qa.q: Whose bags did Anirban carry up four flights?
qa.a: He carried old Mr Sen's bags.

qa.q: Why did Rehana keep calling Anirban 'the crybaby'?
qa.a: Rehana felt certain after the first day, and that early picture anchored her story about him, so later brave acts didn't change the label.

qa.q: What could Rehana do to see Anirban more fairly?
qa.a: She could list what she has seen since that first day, like the running, the bags and the dog, and ask whether the old label still fits.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel hearing 'Not the crybaby' every time teams are picked?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and left out, still judged by one hard moving day.

grounding: Shows a child sticking to a first-day label for a new neighbour despite weeks of different behaviour.

passage:
"Nikita didi, the new boy is so rude."
"Why, Francis?"
"On the first day he didn't say hi to anyone. He just sat in the corner."
"And since then?"
"Well... yesterday he shared his colours with me. And today he helped Sunil find his bottle."
"That doesn't sound rude."
"But on the first day he was."
"Maybe he was scared on the first day. New school, new city."
"Hmm. But I already told everyone he's rude."
"So is it more important to be right or to be fair?"
"...Fair."
"What would you think if today was your first day meeting him?"
"That he's nice. He's funny, actually. He does bird noises."
"So which one is the real him?"
"Maybe both. But mostly the colours one."

qa.q: What did the new boy share with Francis yesterday?
qa.a: He shared his colours with Francis.

qa.q: Why does Francis keep calling the new boy rude?
qa.a: Francis feels stuck on the first-day picture and a bit embarrassed at having already told everyone, so later kindness doesn't change the opinion.

qa.q: How does Nikita didi help Francis rethink?
qa.a: She asks what Francis would think if today were the first meeting, which lets later behaviour count as much as the first day.

qa.q: How might the new boy have felt on his first day?
qa.a: He was probably scared and shy in a new school and city, which is why he sat quietly in the corner.

grounding: Shows a child sticking to a first-day opinion that a new classmate is rude, though later behaviour shows kindness.

passage: On the first day of Class 5, a new boy called Hemant came in late, dropped his bag loudly and laughed when the teacher said his name wrong. I'm Vaibhav, and I decided right then that he was a show-off. For the next month, whatever Hemant did, I saw the show-off. When he gave me half his samosa after I forgot my lunch, I thought it was a trick. Then his mother came to school on Parents' Day, and I heard her say they had moved three times in two years. Hemant had been nervous that first morning. The laugh was nerves. I looked at everything again. He wasn't a show-off. He was just kind, and a bit loud.

qa.q: What did Hemant give Vaibhav after Vaibhav forgot lunch?
qa.a: Half his samosa.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav see every kind act as showing off?
qa.a: Vaibhav had felt annoyed on the first day and was sure of that first picture, so every later act was bent to fit it.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav do on meeting someone new next time?
qa.a: Treat the first-day opinion as a guess and let later actions, like sharing food or helping, change the view.

qa.q: How might Hemant have felt on his first morning?
qa.a: Hemant was likely nervous after moving three times in two years, and laughed out of nerves.

grounding: A child looks back on judging a new classmate by his first day and sticking with it though his later kindness showed otherwise.

passage:
Class 4 observation note, 25 July.
Harish joined us three weeks ago. On his first day he cried at lunch, and some children, Chinmay among them, called him "a baby."
Since then he has settled well. He scored highest in the maths quiz, he organised a game of kho-kho at break, and he stood up for a younger child in the corridor. Yet today, when I asked Chinmay to pair with Harish for the science project, he said, "Not with the baby." When I asked why, he said, "He cries." I asked when. "On the first day." Nothing since.
I have asked Chinmay to write three things Harish has done this week. We will read them together tomorrow. I will also pair them for one task.

qa.q: When did Harish cry at lunch?
qa.a: On his first day.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay not want to pair with Harish?
qa.a: Chinmay still felt sure Harish was a baby because of the first day, and felt embarrassed to change that view even though nothing since supported it.

qa.q: What is the teacher's plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: Asking Chinmay to write three things Harish did this week and pairing them for a task, so Chinmay sees Harish as he is now.

qa.q: How might Harish feel being called a baby three weeks later?
qa.a: Harish might feel hurt and stuck, since he has done so much since then and is still judged by one hard day.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child still judging a new classmate by his first-day tears, though later behaviour is very different.

passage:
Friday, the second week after the summer holidays. It rained all day.
Dear diary, the new girl Disha is still bossy. On the first day she said my shoes were muddy and I should sit somewhere else. I told everybody she's bossy.
Today she lent me her umbrella when mine blew inside out. Yesterday she explained fractions to the boy who sits behind me. On Tuesday she shared her lunch with a girl who forgot her tiffin.
But she's still bossy. I decided on the first day.
Hmm. Amma asked what bossy thing Disha did this week. I couldn't think of one. Only the shoes thing, and that was two weeks ago. Maybe the shoes thing was first-day nerves. Maybe I'm the one who's stuck.
Santosh

qa.q: What did Disha lend on Friday?
qa.a: Disha lent her umbrella when Santosh's blew inside out.

qa.q: Why does Santosh still think Disha is bossy?
qa.a: Santosh felt stung by the first-day comment about muddy shoes, and that early feeling stuck even as later kind acts piled up.

qa.q: What question from Amma helped, and what could Santosh do next?
qa.a: Asking what bossy thing Disha did this week showed there was none; Santosh could now tell friends about the umbrella and the lunch too.

qa.q: How might Disha feel if she knew she was still called bossy?
qa.a: Disha might feel hurt and puzzled, having been kind all week after one nervous first-day remark.

grounding: Shows a child who forms an opinion of a new classmate on the first day and holds on to it though later behaviour differs.

passage:
In the winter term, a new girl joined the village school near Bhadrak. Her name was Uma, and on the first day she didn't say one word to anyone. At lunch she ate alone under the peepal tree.
"She thinks she's too good for us," Irfan announced. "City girl. Proud."
Over the next weeks Uma helped the little ones carry water and gave Irfan her spare pencil when his broke during a test.
But whenever anyone mentioned her, Irfan said, "Proud, na?" It felt like a fact he had found out on day one.
At the Makar Sankranti kite contest, their kites tangled. Untangling the strings, Uma said quietly, "My first day, I was so scared I couldn't speak."
Irfan let go of his string. Scared. He had never even thought of scared.

qa.q: Where did Uma eat lunch on her first day?
qa.a: Uma ate alone under the peepal tree.

qa.q: Why did Irfan keep calling Uma proud?
qa.a: Irfan felt confident the first day had shown the truth, so even the spare pencil and the help with water didn't shift that early picture.

qa.q: What could Irfan do the next time someone new is silent on the first day?
qa.a: Irfan could treat the first-day impression as a guess and watch what the person does over the next weeks, or simply ask.

qa.q: What was the first day like for Uma?
qa.a: Uma was so scared she couldn't speak and ate alone, which Irfan read as pride.

grounding: Shows a child who decides on a new classmate's first day that she is proud and keeps that story despite later kindness.

passage:
On the first cold morning of the winter term in Cape Town, a new girl called Zanele bumped into Mei in the lunch queue and knocked her soup tray to the floor. "Sorry," Zanele muttered, and hurried off.
"She's mean," Mei told her table. "She did it on purpose."
For three weeks Mei watched Zanele, and everything seemed to fit. When Zanele sat alone, Mei thought: mean. When Zanele didn't laugh at a joke: mean.
She didn't count the day Zanele picked up her dropped mittens and put them on her desk. Or when Zanele clapped loudest after Mei's poem.
At the end of the month, the teacher paired them for a project. Zanele said, "I've wanted to say sorry properly since the soup. I was so nervous that day I couldn't see straight."
Mei looked at her. She thought about the mittens, and felt her cheeks go warm.

qa.q: What did Zanele knock over in the lunch queue?
qa.a: Zanele knocked Mei's soup tray to the floor.

qa.q: Why did everything Zanele did seem to prove she was mean?
qa.a: Mei felt hurt and annoyed after the soup, and that first picture made later actions fit it while the kind acts were ignored.

qa.q: What could Mei do when a first meeting goes badly?
qa.a: Mei could notice the kind acts too, like the mittens and the clapping, and give the person a second chance before deciding.

qa.q: What was the first day like for Zanele?
qa.a: Zanele was so nervous she couldn't see straight, and had wanted to apologise properly for weeks.

grounding: Shows a child whose first impression of a new classmate anchors her view even when later behaviour differs.

passage:
Noor joined Class 4B in January, while paper snowflakes from the winter fair still hung in the school hall. On her first morning she came in late, cheeks red from the cold, and snapped "No!" when Simran offered to share a bench.
"She's rude," Simran told her friends at lunch.
Over the next weeks Noor lent out her glue stick, clapped loudest at the class play and helped Simran pick up a spilled box of beads. Simran mumbled thanks but still whispered, "She's only nice when Miss is watching."
When the teacher paired them for the science chart, Simran's shoulders sagged. Anyone but the rude girl, she thought.

qa.q: What did Noor say when Simran offered to share a bench?
qa.a: Noor snapped "No!" when Simran offered to share a bench.

qa.q: Why does Simran keep calling Noor rude, even after the glue stick and the beads?
qa.a: Simran felt hurt by that first "No!", and now she feels sure she already knows who Noor is, so kind acts look like a show to her.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Simran look past the first day?
qa.a: The teacher could ask Simran to name three things Noor has done since January, like lending her glue stick, and talk about how that first cold, late morning might have felt.

qa.q: What might the first day have been like for Noor?
qa.a: Noor was new, late and cold, so she may have been nervous and snapped without meaning to be unkind, and then found it hard to change how others saw her.

grounding: Shows a child whose first-day opinion of a new classmate stays fixed even when the classmate's later behaviour is kind.
